intro: I'm Dr. Lena Vasquez, and I study how speech works — what makes your voice sound like you. Every sound you make is a vibration, and that vibration has a shape. A spectrogram turns that shape into a picture: time on one axis, pitch on the other, brightness for loudness. Different vowels make different shapes. Same vowel, different person — same shape, different signature. Today you'll see your own voice as a picture, discover the math hiding inside it, and find out what makes you sound like you.
act1Start: Before we record you, listen to two reference vowels. 'AH' as in 'father' and 'EE' as in 'see.' Watch the spectrograms as they play — notice where the bright bands appear. Those bands are called formants, and they're your first clue that every vowel has a mathematical fingerprint.
act2Capture: Time to capture your own voice. Say each vowel into the mic — hold it for a second or two. Watch your spectrogram build in real time. Don't worry about singing perfectly; your natural voice is exactly what we want. The shape you see is unique to you.
act3Math: A single note is just one sine wave. Your voice is dozens of sine waves stacked together — the fundamental pitch plus harmonics at multiples of that frequency. What makes 'AH' and 'EE' look different on a spectrogram is which harmonics are louder. That's the math. The formants are just the harmonics your mouth amplifies.
act3Closing: Every voice is a sum of sine waves — different fundamentals, different harmonic stacks, different formant shapes. The math is the same for everyone: add enough sine waves at the right frequencies and amplitudes, and you can build any vowel, any voice, any sound in the world. That's the connection between trigonometry and the sound of your own voice.
